Native payment buttons: ApplePayButton (iOS) and GooglePayButton (Android). Use the one that matches the platform; the library does not render both on the same screen.
Renders the system Apple Pay button. Only available on iOS.

Prop Type Required Description buttonType ApplePayButtonType Yes Button label type. buttonStyle ApplePayButtonStyle Yes Visual style. onPress () => void, wrapped with callback() No Called when the user taps the button. Must be wrapped, see Nitro and onPress. style ViewStyle No Layout/style (e.g. width, height). ApplePayButtonType: 'buy' | 'setUp' | 'book' | 'donate' | 'continue' | 'reload' | 'addMoney' | 'topUp' | 'order' | 'rent' | 'support' | 'contribute' | 'tip' ApplePayButtonStyle: 'white' | 'whiteOutline' | 'black'

import { ApplePayButton } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' const handlePayment = async () => { // Call startPayment() from usePaymentCheckout here } <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(handlePayment)} style={{ width: '100%', height: 48 }} />

ApplePayButton is a Nitro view, so onPress must be wrapped with callback() from react-native-nitro-modules. A bare function does not reach the native button, and tapping it does nothing. See Troubleshooting: Nitro callback for onPress.
Renders the Google Pay button. Only available on Android.

Prop Type Required Description buttonType GooglePayButtonType Yes Button label type. theme 'dark' | 'light' Yes Button theme. radius number No Corner radius in dp. onPress () => void, wrapped with callback() No Called when the user taps the button. Must be wrapped, see Nitro and onPress. style ViewStyle No Layout/style (e.g. width, height). GooglePayButtonType: 'buy' | 'book' | 'checkout' | 'donate' | 'order' | 'pay' | 'subscribe' | 'plain'

import { GooglePayButton } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' const handlePayment = async () => { // Call startPayment() from usePaymentCheckout here } <GooglePayButton buttonType="buy" theme="dark" radius={8} onPress={callback(handlePayment)} style={{ width: '100%', height: 48 }} />
Same as Apple: onPress must be wrapped, as in onPress={callback(handlePayment)}. See Troubleshooting: Nitro callback for onPress.

Render one button per platform: import { Platform } from 'react-native' import { ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' const handlePayment = async () => { // Call startPayment() from usePaymentCheckout here } const style = { width: '100%', height: 48 } as const {Platform.OS === 'ios' ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(handlePayment)} style={style} /> ) : ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="buy" theme="dark" onPress={callback(handlePayment)} style={style} /> )}
usePaymentCheckout — Hook that provides cart and startPayment HybridPaymentHandler — Low-level API
Low-level API for payment operations. Use it when you need full control over the payment request and do not want the cart/state from usePaymentCheckout.
import { HybridPaymentHandler, createPaymentRequest } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay'

Synchronously returns whether the payment service is available on the device. import { HybridPaymentHandler } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const status = HybridPaymentHandler.payServiceStatus() // status: { canMakePayments: boolean, canSetupCards: boolean } canMakePayments — User can complete a payment (has a valid card, etc.). canSetupCards — User can add or manage cards (e.g. Wallet settings).

Starts the native payment flow with the given request. Returns a promise that resolves with the payment result. Pass the request through normalizePaymentRequest (or build it with createPaymentRequest) so amounts are validated before the sheet opens. See PaymentAmount. import { HybridPaymentHandler, normalizePaymentRequest } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const result = await HybridPaymentHandler.startPayment( normalizePaymentRequest({ merchantName: 'Your Store', countryCode: 'US', currencyCode: 'USD', merchantCapabilities: ['3DS'], supportedNetworks: ['visa', 'mastercard', 'amex'], paymentItems: [{ label: 'Coffee Subscription', amount: '29.99', type: 'final' }], googlePayMerchantId: 'your_google_pay_merchant_id', }) ) // result: PaymentResult PaymentResult: interface PaymentResult { success: boolean transactionId?: string token?: PaymentToken error?: string } options.onAuthorize charges the token before the Apple Pay sheet closes. The result follows your callback: const result = await HybridPaymentHandler.startPayment(request, { onAuthorize: async (token) => { const charged = await chargeOnServer(token) return charged ? { status: 'success' } : { status: 'failure', error: 'Payment failed' } }, }) See Charge before the sheet closes for the timeout and Android behavior. On iOS, the merchant ID is resolved from the app entitlements by default. Use applePayMerchantIdentifier only when you need to override the configured value at runtime. On iOS, the Apple Pay sheet lists your paymentItems and then a total labelled with merchantName ("Pay Your Store"). The library adds that total for you, so don't add your own "Total" item. Without merchantName, the total uses your app's display name. Build the request yourself or use createPaymentRequest for a single line item with defaults. Only one payment can be in flight at a time. A call made while another payment is still in progress, including one started by usePaymentCheckout, resolves immediately with { success: false, error: 'A payment is already in progress' } and does not affect the payment in flight. This applies on iOS and Android. With onAuthorize, the payment stays in flight until your callback settles.

Returns whether the user can make payments with the given card networks. import { HybridPaymentHandler } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const canPay = HybridPaymentHandler.canMakePayments(['visa', 'mastercard'])

Custom checkout flow without the hook’s cart. One-off payments where you already have a full PaymentRequest. Flows that need full request control (for example shippingType, shippingMethods, billingContactRequired, or shippingContactRequired). Need to check availability or supported networks without using usePaymentCheckout. For most apps, usePaymentCheckout is simpler: it builds the request from the cart and manages state.
createPaymentRequest — Build a request with defaults Types — PaymentRequest, PaymentResult, PaymentToken
TypeScript types exported from @gmisoftware/react-native-pay. Use them for request/result handling and server integration.

A monetary amount in the currency's major unit (dollars, not cents). type PaymentAmount = number | string Decimal string ('19.99'): exact. Must match ^-?\d+(\.\d+)?$; no exponents, spaces, or thousands separators. Number (19.99): read as the shortest decimal that round-trips, so 19.99 stays exactly 19.99. Results of float arithmetic such as 0.1 + 0.2 (0.30000000000000004) fail validation instead of being rounded. Before a payment starts, every amount is validated and sent to native code as a decimal string with the currency's number of decimal places (ISO 4217: 2 for USD, 0 for JPY, 3 for KWD). Native code converts it with NSDecimalNumber (iOS) and BigDecimal (Android), never through Double. A payment does not start when: an amount is not a finite number or a plain decimal string (NaN, Infinity, 'abc'); an amount has more decimal places than the currency allows (1.005 in USD, '1200.5' in JPY); the total of paymentItems is negative. Negative line items (discounts) are allowed. Google Pay accepts at most two decimal places, so on Android a three-decimal amount such as '1.234' KWD fails with an error.

A single line item (label, amount, type). interface PaymentItem { label: string amount: PaymentAmount // number | string type: 'final' | 'pending' } type is exported as PaymentItemType. final — Confirmed amount (e.g. product price, tax). pending — Estimate (e.g. shipping that may change). If any item is pending, the total is an estimate too: Google Pay receives totalPriceStatus: 'ESTIMATED' and Apple Pay marks the total summary item as .pending. Every item is sent to Google Pay as a LINE_ITEM display item, with status set to FINAL or PENDING.

Full request passed to the native layer (or to HybridPaymentHandler.startPayment). interface PaymentRequest { applePayMerchantIdentifier?: string merchantName?: string countryCode: string currencyCode: string paymentItems: PaymentItem[] merchantCapabilities: string[] supportedNetworks: string[] shippingType?: string shippingMethods?: PaymentItem[] billingContactRequired?: boolean shippingContactRequired?: boolean // Google Pay (Android) googlePayMerchantId?: string googlePayEnvironment?: 'TEST' | 'PRODUCTION' googlePayGateway?: string googlePayGatewayMerchantId?: string } On iOS, applePayMerchantIdentifier is optional and only needed when you want to override the Merchant ID configured in the native app entitlements. merchantName is the business name shown to the payer: the name on the Google Pay sheet and the label of the Apple Pay total. Apple Pay shows the last summary item as the total ("Pay label"), so on iOS the library appends a total item labelled with merchantName after your paymentItems, also when there is only one item. Don't add your own "Total" item. If merchantName is missing or blank, Android uses the app's label from the manifest and iOS uses the app's display name (CFBundleDisplayName, then CFBundleName).

Returned from startPayment() (hook or handler). interface PaymentResult { success: boolean transactionId?: string token?: PaymentToken error?: string } Send token (and optionally transactionId) to your backend to complete the charge with your gateway.

Optional second argument of HybridPaymentHandler.startPayment(). The hook takes onAuthorize in its config instead. interface StartPaymentOptions { onAuthorize?: (token: PaymentToken) => Promise<PaymentAuthorizationResult> } interface PaymentAuthorizationResult { status: 'success' | 'failure' error?: string // becomes PaymentResult.error on failure } See Charge before the sheet closes.

The token you send to your server. Do not log or expose; treat as sensitive. interface PaymentToken { paymentMethod: PaymentMethod transactionIdentifier: string paymentData: string // Opaque token payload (format depends on platform + gateway) } paymentMethod — Card/network and optional billing contact. transactionIdentifier — Unique id for this payment session. paymentData — Opaque payload for your gateway. iOS: Base64-encoded Apple Pay token data. Android: Google Pay tokenization payload (tokenizationData.token), gateway-dependent.

Describes the selected payment instrument. interface PaymentMethod { displayName?: string network?: PaymentNetwork type: PaymentMethodType secureElementPass?: PKSecureElementPass // iOS billingAddress?: CNContact // iOS } type PaymentMethodType = 'unknown' | 'debit' | 'credit' | 'prepaid' | 'store' PaymentMethodType is exported separately for direct typing.
Supported card networks. type PaymentNetwork = | 'visa' | 'mastercard' | 'amex' | 'discover' | 'jcb' | 'maestro' | 'electron' | 'elo' | 'idcredit' | 'interac' | 'privateLabel'
Returned by HybridPaymentHandler.payServiceStatus(). interface PayServiceStatus { canMakePayments: boolean canSetupCards: boolean }
Used in config and PaymentRequest for Android. type GooglePayEnvironment = 'TEST' | 'PRODUCTION' Use 'TEST' for development/sandbox; 'PRODUCTION' for live charges.

These iOS-only types appear in payment-related metadata returned by Apple Pay APIs (for example pass details tied to the selected card) and are mostly useful in advanced/native-integrated flows. type PassActivationState = | 'activated' | 'requiresActivation' | 'activating' | 'suspended' | 'deactivated' interface PKPass { passTypeIdentifier: string serialNumber: string organizationName?: string } interface PKSecureElementPass extends PKPass { primaryAccountIdentifier: string primaryAccountNumberSuffix: string deviceAccountIdentifier: string deviceAccountNumberSuffix: string passActivationState: PassActivationState devicePassIdentifier?: string pairedTerminalIdentifier?: string }

Used on iOS when billingContactRequired / shippingContactRequired is requested in PaymentRequest. These fields are populated from the contact information the user approves in the Apple Pay sheet. type CNContactType = 'person' | 'organization' interface CNPhoneNumber { stringValue: string } interface CNPostalAddress { street?: string city?: string state?: string postalCode?: string country?: string isoCountryCode?: string } interface CNLabeledPhoneNumber { label?: string value: CNPhoneNumber } interface CNLabeledEmailAddress { label?: string value: string } interface CNLabeledPostalAddress { label?: string value: CNPostalAddress } interface CNContact { identifier: string contactType: CNContactType namePrefix: string givenName: string middleName: string familyName: string previousFamilyName: string nameSuffix: string nickname: string organizationName: string departmentName: string jobTitle: string phoneticGivenName: string phoneticMiddleName: string phoneticFamilyName: string phoneticOrganizationName?: string note: string imageDataAvailable?: boolean phoneNumbers: CNLabeledPhoneNumber[] emailAddresses: CNLabeledEmailAddress[] postalAddresses: CNLabeledPostalAddress[] }
type ApplePayStatus = PayServiceStatus
The main hook for payment checkout. It handles availability, cart state, and payment processing so you can focus on UI and sending the token to your server.
import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay'

Pass a single config object. iOS reads the Apple Pay merchant ID from the native app configuration. Use applePayMerchantIdentifier only if you need to override it at runtime. Source of truth for these types: package/src/hooks/usePaymentCheckout.ts. interface UsePaymentCheckoutConfig { merchantName?: string // business name shown on the sheet countryCode?: string // default: 'US' currencyCode?: string // default: 'USD' supportedNetworks?: string[] // default: ['visa', 'mastercard', 'amex', 'discover'] merchantCapabilities?: string[] // default: ['3DS'] applePayMerchantIdentifier?: string // optional iOS override // Google Pay (Android) googlePayMerchantId?: string googlePayEnvironment?: 'TEST' | 'PRODUCTION' googlePayGateway?: string googlePayGatewayMerchantId?: string // Charge the token before the sheet closes onAuthorize?: (token: PaymentToken) => Promise<PaymentAuthorizationResult> } merchantName — The business name shown to the payer. On iOS, Apple Pay labels the total with it, so the sheet reads "Pay merchantName". On Android, it is the merchant name on the Google Pay sheet. Without it, iOS uses your app's display name (CFBundleDisplayName) and Android uses the app's label. Set it on both platforms. onAuthorize — Called with the token after the user authorizes the payment. Charge it on your server and resolve with { status: 'success' } or { status: 'failure', error }. See Charge before the sheet closes.

interface UsePaymentCheckoutReturn { // Availability canMakePayments: boolean canSetupCards: boolean isCheckingStatus: boolean // Cart items: PaymentItem[] total: number addItem: (label: string, amount: PaymentAmount, type?: 'final' | 'pending') => void addItems: (items: Array<{ label: string; amount: PaymentAmount; type?: 'final' | 'pending' }>) => void removeItem: (index: number) => void updateItem: (index: number, updates: Partial<PaymentItem>) => void clearItems: () => void // Payment startPayment: () => Promise<PaymentResult | null> isProcessing: boolean result: PaymentResult | null error: Error | null // Utilities reset: () => void paymentRequest: PaymentRequest } canMakePayments — Whether the user can pay with Apple Pay / Google Pay on this device. canSetupCards — Whether the user can add or manage cards (e.g. in Wallet). isCheckingStatus — true while availability is being checked on mount. items / total — Current cart and its exact decimal total, as a number (NaN if an amount is invalid). Amounts are number | string (PaymentAmount); use formatAmount(item.amount, currencyCode) to display them. startPayment() — Opens the native sheet. Returns Promise<PaymentResult | null>. Returns null and sets error when the cart is empty. Returns null and sets error, without opening the sheet, when an amount is invalid or the total is negative (see PaymentAmount). Returns PaymentResult (including { success: false, error }) when the native flow completes with a failure result. Returns null if an exception is thrown while starting/processing the payment. With onAuthorize, resolves after your callback settles. A 'failure' result becomes { success: false, error } and sets error. Returns { success: false, error: 'A payment is already in progress' } without opening a second sheet if a payment is still in flight: If the payment in flight was started by this hook, the hook state is not changed. If it was started elsewhere (HybridPaymentHandler or another usePaymentCheckout), the native handler rejects the call and the hook records it like any failed payment, in result and error. reset() — Clears result and error (does not clear cart). It does not clear isProcessing while a payment is in flight; isProcessing becomes false when that payment settles.

import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const { canMakePayments, items, total, addItem, addItems, removeItem, startPayment, isProcessing, error, reset, } = usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', currencyCode: 'USD', countryCode: 'US', googlePayMerchantId: 'your_google_pay_merchant_id', googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST', googlePayGateway: 'stripe', googlePayGatewayMerchantId: 'your_stripe_merchant_id', }) // Single item addItem('Product', 29.99) // Multiple items; amounts can be numbers or decimal strings addItems([ { label: 'Product', amount: 29.99 }, { label: 'Shipping', amount: '5.00' }, { label: 'Tax', amount: 2.8, type: 'final' }, ]) const result = await startPayment() if (result?.success && result.token) { // Send result.token to your server }
If you call startPayment() when items.length === 0, the hook sets error to a “Cart is empty” error and returns null. Add at least one item before starting payment.

Use usePaymentCheckout when you want cart state + defaults managed in React state. Use HybridPaymentHandler when you need to build the full PaymentRequest yourself (for example custom shipping/contact requirements or prebuilt request payloads from your backend). Utility helpers for this path are documented in Utility functions.
Components (ApplePayButton / GooglePayButton) HybridPaymentHandler — Low-level API Types — PaymentItem, PaymentResult, PaymentRequest, etc.
Helpers for building payment requests, items, and formatting. All are exported from @gmisoftware/react-native-pay.

Use these functions when you are building a manual or low-level flow (usually with HybridPaymentHandler) and need to assemble PaymentRequest data yourself. If you use usePaymentCheckout, cart state and request building are handled for you internally, so these helpers are optional.

Builds a full PaymentRequest with one line item and sensible defaults. Required: amount, label. Defaults: countryCode: 'US', currencyCode: 'USD', supportedNetworks: [CommonNetworks], merchantCapabilities: ['3DS']. The amount is validated with normalizePaymentRequest, so createPaymentRequest throws for an invalid amount, and the returned request holds it as a decimal string. import { createPaymentRequest } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const request = createPaymentRequest({ amount: 29.99, // or '29.99' label: 'Coffee Subscription', merchantName: 'Your Store', countryCode: 'US', currencyCode: 'USD', // Optional: applePayMerchantIdentifier, googlePayMerchantId, // googlePayEnvironment, googlePayGateway, googlePayGatewayMerchantId, etc. }) // request.paymentItems is a single item: [{ label: 'Coffee Subscription', amount: '29.99', type: 'final' }] Use with HybridPaymentHandler.startPayment(request) for a manual flow.

Validates every amount in paymentItems and shippingMethods and returns a copy in which each amount is a decimal string with the currency's number of decimal places. See PaymentAmount for the rules. Call it before passing a request you built yourself to HybridPaymentHandler.startPayment. createPaymentRequest and usePaymentCheckout already call it. import { HybridPaymentHandler, normalizePaymentRequest } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const request = normalizePaymentRequest({ countryCode: 'US', currencyCode: 'USD', paymentItems: [ { label: 'Book', amount: 19.9, type: 'final' }, { label: 'Discount', amount: '-5', type: 'final' }, ], supportedNetworks: ['visa', 'mastercard'], merchantCapabilities: ['3DS'], }) // request.paymentItems amounts: '19.90', '-5.00' await HybridPaymentHandler.startPayment(request) normalizePaymentRequest({ ...request, paymentItems: [{ label: 'Fee', amount: 1.005, type: 'final' }] }) // throws: Amount for "Fee" has more than 2 decimal places, which USD allows, got 1.005

Creates a single PaymentItem. import { createPaymentItem } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' createPaymentItem('Subscription', 29.99, 'final') createPaymentItem('Shipping', '5.00', 'pending') // type defaults to 'final' The amount is stored as given and validated when the payment starts.

Sums the amount of all items with exact decimal arithmetic, the same as native code, and returns the sum as a number. Returns NaN if an amount is invalid. import { calculateTotal, createPaymentItem } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const items = [ createPaymentItem('Product', 29.99), createPaymentItem('Tax', '2.40'), ] calculateTotal(items) // 32.39 calculateTotal([createPaymentItem('A', 0.1), createPaymentItem('B', 0.2)]) // 0.3, not 0.30000000000000004

Formats a number or decimal string with the currency's number of decimal places (two when currencyCode is omitted), rounding half away from zero. Returns 'NaN' for an invalid amount. import { formatAmount } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' formatAmount(29.9) // "29.90" formatAmount('100') // "100.00" formatAmount(1.005) // "1.01" formatAmount(1500, 'JPY') // "1500"
Parses a string to a number. import { parseAmount } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' parseAmount('29.99') // 29.99 parseAmount('100') // 100

Returns whether network is in supportedNetworks (case-insensitive). import { isNetworkSupported } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' isNetworkSupported('visa', ['visa', 'mastercard']) // true isNetworkSupported('AMEX', ['visa', 'amex']) // true isNetworkSupported('discover', ['visa', 'mastercard']) // false

Returns a human-readable name for a payment network. import { formatNetworkName } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' formatNetworkName('visa') // "Visa" formatNetworkName('amex') // "American Express" formatNetworkName('mastercard') // "Mastercard"

Constants for common network IDs (for building supportedNetworks): import { CommonNetworks } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' CommonNetworks.VISA // 'visa' CommonNetworks.MASTERCARD // 'mastercard' CommonNetworks.AMEX // 'amex' CommonNetworks.DISCOVER // 'discover' Use with createPaymentRequest or when building a PaymentRequest by hand.
Supported versions and upgrade notes.

react — * (compatible with current React 18/19) react-native — * (0.70+ recommended) react-native-nitro-modules — >= 0.36.0 (required) expo — >= 53.0.0 (if using Expo; tested with SDK 57 / React Native 0.86) Android minSdkVersion — 26+ (required for Nitro Modules prefab) Install the correct Nitro version first; the payment library depends on it.
React Native 0.70 or newer (0.86 with Expo SDK 57) Expo 53–57 when using Expo

merchantIdentifier — Optional in the plugin config. If omitted, Apple Pay entitlements are not added (use for Android-only or when you add Apple Pay later). enableGooglePay — Defaults to false. Set to true to enable Google Pay on Android.

Platform Apple Pay Google Pay iOS Yes (ApplePayButton, usePaymentCheckout, HybridPaymentHandler) N/A (use Google Pay on Android) Android N/A Yes (GooglePayButton, usePaymentCheckout, HybridPaymentHandler) Use Platform.OS (or equivalent) to render the correct button and to pass platform-specific config (e.g. Google Pay options only on Android).

Regenerated Nitrogen bindings for react-native-nitro-modules 0.36+ (Expo SDK 57 / React Native 0.86). Peer dependency react-native-nitro-modules is now >= 0.36.0 (was >= 0.35.0). Example app upgraded to Expo SDK 57 (React Native 0.86, React 19.2.3).

Regenerated Nitrogen bindings for react-native-nitro-modules 0.35+ (JavaPart/CxxPart JNI model). Peer dependency react-native-nitro-modules is now >= 0.35.0 (was >= 0.31.4). Android minSdkVersion 26+ is required (Nitro Modules prefab). Set minSdkVersion to at least 26 in expo-build-properties or your app's build.gradle. Consumers on nitro 0.31.x must stay on 0.0.14 or upgrade nitro-modules first. Check the package changelog or GitHub releases for version-specific notes. When upgrading, run npx expo prebuild --clean and re-test on both platforms. If you use TypeScript, run bun run typecheck (or your typecheck script) after upgrading.

Do I need Expo? No. The library works in bare React Native too. The Expo plugin only simplifies adding Apple Pay entitlements and Google Pay metadata; in a bare project you configure those in Xcode and Android Studio yourself. Can I use only Apple Pay or only Google Pay? Yes. Omit enableGooglePay (or set false) for iOS-only; omit plugin merchantIdentifier for Android-only. In code, only render the button for the platform you support. Which gateways are supported for Google Pay? Any gateway that supports the Google Pay API and the gateway token format. Commonly used: Stripe, Braintree, Square, Adyen, Authorize.net, Checkout.com. Set googlePayMerchantId, googlePayGateway, and googlePayGatewayMerchantId accordingly. Where do I report issues? GitHub Issues.
The repository includes a full example app in the example/ folder: an Expo app that demonstrates the checkout flow with usePaymentCheckout, cart management, and platform-specific buttons.

From example/app/(tabs)/index.tsx: import { Platform } from 'react-native' import { ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton, usePaymentCheckout, } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' const { canMakePayments, isCheckingStatus, items, total, addItems, clearItems, startPayment, isProcessing, reset, } = usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', countryCode: 'US', currencyCode: 'USD', }) const handleAddCoffee = () => { clearItems() addItems([ { label: 'Coffee', amount: 4.99 }, { label: 'Tax', amount: 0.5 }, ]) } const handlePayment = async () => { const paymentResult = await startPayment() if (paymentResult?.success) { reset() clearItems() } } {Platform.OS === 'ios' ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(handlePayment)} style={{ width: '100%', height: 56 }} /> ) : ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="buy" theme="dark" radius={8} onPress={callback(handlePayment)} style={{ width: '100%', height: 56 }} /> )}

Checkout flow — Add items (e.g. “Coffee”, “Subscription”), see cart and total, then pay with Apple Pay or Google Pay. Status — Check whether the device can make payments or only set up cards. Cart UI — Add/clear items and display total. Result handling — Success and error messages; reset and clear cart after success. Nitro callback — Buttons use callback(handlePayment) (see Troubleshooting: Nitro callback for onPress).
From the repo root: cd example bun install npx expo prebuild npx expo run:ios # or npx expo run:android Or from the root (if scripts are set up): bun run ios # or bun run android

Use the checkout screen in the example app as a reference for: Calls usePaymentCheckout with countryCode, currencyCode, and optional platform-specific overrides. Shows a loading state while isCheckingStatus is true. Renders “Quick Add” buttons that call addItems or addItem. Displays the cart (items + total) and a “Clear” action. Renders ApplePayButton on iOS and GooglePayButton on Android with callback(handlePayment). On successful payment, shows an alert and calls reset() and clearItems(). Copy these patterns into your app: config setup, cart handling, button usage, and native-safe onPress handlers.
documents.s: What to copy from the example

documents.t: The example’s app.json includes the React Native Pay plugin (e.g. with a demo Merchant ID and Google Pay enabled). Change the plugin merchantIdentifier and any Google Pay runtime settings to your own for real payments.
Quick Start — Minimal integration in your app API: usePaymentCheckout — Hook options and return value Troubleshooting — Common integration issues and fixes
Use the cart API from usePaymentCheckout to add, update, and remove items before calling startPayment().

Single item: addItem('Product name', 29.99) addItem('Discount', -5, 'final') // negative for discounts Multiple items: addItems([ { label: 'Product', amount: 29.99 }, { label: 'Shipping', amount: 5 }, { label: 'Tax', amount: 2.8, type: 'final' }, ])
Change label or amount (or type) by index: updateItem(0, { label: 'Product (x2)', amount: 59.98 })
removeItem(index) // remove one item clearItems() // empty the cart

import { formatAmount, usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const { addItem, clearItems, total } = usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', countryCode: 'US', currencyCode: 'USD', }) // Add product with quantity const handleAddProduct = (name: string, unitPrice: number, quantity: number) => { // 1.1 * 3 is 3.3000000000000003; round it to the currency's decimals addItem(`${name} (×${quantity})`, formatAmount(unitPrice * quantity)) } // Apply percentage discount (a negative line item) const handleApplyDiscount = (percent: number) => { addItem('Discount', formatAmount(-total * (percent / 100)), 'final') } // Clear cart const handleClearCart = () => { clearItems() }

At least one item is required before startPayment(). Otherwise the hook sets an error and returns null. total is derived from items; you don’t set it manually. It is an exact decimal sum. Round computed amounts with formatAmount(value, currencyCode). startPayment() rejects amounts with more decimal places than the currency allows, which includes unrounded float results such as 1.1 * 3. See PaymentAmount. Discounts can be negative line items, as long as the total is not negative. Use type: 'final' for confirmed amounts (e.g. product price, tax); use 'pending' for estimates (e.g. shipping) if your flow supports it. One pending item makes the total an estimate. Google Pay shows the total as estimated (totalPriceStatus: 'ESTIMATED') and Apple Pay marks the total as pending. An estimate does not let you charge a different amount: Google Pay requires the amount you authorize and charge to match the totalPrice shown on the sheet, and a mismatch can be declined. If the final amount differs from the estimate, start a new payment with the final amount, unless your gateway explicitly supports adjusting it (for example, incremental authorization).
Use HybridPaymentHandler and createPaymentRequest when you want full control and do not need the hook’s cart state.

import { HybridPaymentHandler } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const status = HybridPaymentHandler.payServiceStatus() if (!status.canMakePayments) { // Hide the pay button and show "Apple Pay / Google Pay not available" }

Either use a helper or build the object yourself: import { createPaymentRequest, HybridPaymentHandler } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const paymentRequest = createPaymentRequest({ amount: 99.99, label: 'Premium Subscription', merchantName: 'Your Store', countryCode: 'US', currencyCode: 'USD', googlePayMerchantId: 'your_google_pay_merchant_id', googlePayEnvironment: 'PRODUCTION', googlePayGateway: 'stripe', googlePayGatewayMerchantId: 'your_merchant_id', }) createPaymentRequest throws if the amount is invalid (see PaymentAmount). For multiple line items, build paymentItems yourself and pass the full PaymentRequest through normalizePaymentRequest, which applies the same checks. On iOS, the Merchant ID is read from the app entitlements unless you explicitly pass applePayMerchantIdentifier.

const handlePayment = async () => { try { const result = await HybridPaymentHandler.startPayment(paymentRequest) if (result.success && result.token) { await sendTokenToServer(result.token, result.transactionId) } else { console.error('Payment failed:', result.error) } } catch (err) { console.error('Payment error:', err) } } To charge the token before the Apple Pay sheet closes, pass startPayment(paymentRequest, { onAuthorize }) and charge inside the callback instead of calling sendTokenToServer afterwards, so the token isn't charged twice. See Charge before the sheet closes.

Use the platform-specific button, and pass it status.canMakePayments from step 1 so it stays hidden when payments are unavailable. Its onPress must be wrapped with callback() from react-native-nitro-modules, or the tap does nothing: import { Platform } from 'react-native' import { ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' function PaymentButton({ canMakePayments, handlePayment, }: { canMakePayments: boolean handlePayment: () => Promise<void> }) { if (!canMakePayments) return null return Platform.OS === 'ios' ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(handlePayment)} /> ) : ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="subscribe" theme="dark" onPress={callback(handlePayment)} /> ) }

One-off or fixed-amount payments (e.g. subscription, tip). You already have a cart elsewhere and only need to build a PaymentRequest once. You want to avoid the hook’s internal state. For cart-based checkout, usePaymentCheckout is usually simpler.
After a successful payment, your app receives a token and optional transactionId. Your backend must use this token with your payment gateway (Stripe, Braintree, etc.) to create the charge.

From the client, send at least: token — The full PaymentToken object (or the fields your gateway needs). Treat as sensitive. transactionId — From PaymentResult.transactionId, for idempotency or logging. amount (and currency) — So the server can validate and charge the correct amount. Any order/cart id — So the server knows what was purchased. Example: import { useEffect } from 'react' import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const order = { id: 'order_123', label: 'Premium plan', total: '49.99' } // your order function useOrderPayment() { const { addItem, clearItems, startPayment, total } = usePaymentCheckout({ currencyCode: 'USD', }) // Fill the cart before the user taps pay: startPayment() returns null // for an empty cart, and items added in the same handler arrive too late. useEffect(() => { addItem(order.label, order.total) return clearItems }, [addItem, clearItems]) // Pass this to the pay button's onPress, wrapped with callback(). return async () => { const result = await startPayment() if (result?.success && result.token) { const response = await fetch('https://api.yourserver.com/process-payment', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ token: result.token, transactionId: result.transactionId, amount: total, currency: 'USD', orderId: order.id, }), }) if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Payment processing failed') } } }
documents.s: What to send to the server

documents.t: Without onAuthorize, Apple Pay shows its success checkmark as soon as the user authorizes, before your server has charged anything. If the charge then fails, the user has already seen "Done". Pass onAuthorize to charge the token while the sheet waits. Resolve with the outcome, and the sheet shows success or failure: import { useEffect } from 'react' import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' const order = { id: 'order_123', label: 'Premium plan', total: '49.99' } // your order function useOrderPayment() { const { addItem, clearItems, startPayment } = usePaymentCheckout({ currencyCode: 'USD', onAuthorize: async (token) => { const response = await fetch('https://api.yourserver.com/process-payment', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ token, amount: order.total, currency: 'USD', orderId: order.id }), }) if (!response.ok) { const { error } = await response.json() return { status: 'failure', error } } return { status: 'success' } }, }) useEffect(() => { addItem(order.label, order.total) return clearItems }, [addItem, clearItems]) return async () => { const result = await startPayment() // result.success is true only when onAuthorize returned 'success'. // The token is already charged, so don't send it to your server again. } } With HybridPaymentHandler, pass the same callback as startPayment(request, { onAuthorize }). How it behaves: Failure: { status: 'failure', error } makes the sheet show the failure state. startPayment resolves with success: false and your error. A rejected promise is treated the same way. Retries on iOS: if the user retries from the sheet after a failure or a timeout, onAuthorize runs again with the new token. The result reflects the last attempt. A retry can start while a timed-out charge is still running, so key idempotency on your order ID, not on the token. Timeout: onAuthorize must settle within 25 seconds (Apple Pay itself gives up after about 30). Otherwise the payment fails with "Payment authorization timed out" and the late result is ignored. Your server may still have charged the card, so make the charge idempotent and reconcile by order ID. Android: Google Pay closes its sheet before it returns the token, and its basic flow has no step that waits for the merchant. onAuthorize still runs, with the same timeout, after the sheet closes, and its outcome decides the PaymentResult. The same callback works on both platforms.

Your backend receives the token and calls your gateway SDK/API. The exact request body and field mapping depend on your gateway + tokenization mode. Treat this example as shape guidance, not drop-in code. // Backend (Node.js example) app.post('/process-payment', async (req, res) => { const { token, amount, currency, orderId } = req.body try { // 1) Validate order/cart server-side (amount, currency, ownership, status) // 2) Choose gateway flow based on platform/gateway config // - iOS (Apple Pay): paymentData is Apple token payload (Base64 string) // - Android (Google Pay): paymentData is Google tokenization payload // 3) Call gateway API with the exact fields required by that provider // 4) Use idempotency keys and persist payment state const charge = await gateway.charge({ amountMinor: Math.round(amount * 100), currency, tokenPayload: token.paymentData, token: token, orderId, transactionId: token.transactionIdentifier, }) res.json({ success: true, chargeId: charge.id }) } catch (err) { res.status(500).json({ error: err.message }) } }) Important: Use your gateway’s official docs for: Mapping PaymentToken fields to provider-specific request fields. Creating a payment method/source/intent from Apple Pay or Google Pay token payloads. Idempotency (e.g. using transactionId to avoid duplicate charges). Handling failures and refunds. Provider-specific walkthroughs in Przelewy24 Apple Pay + Google Pay cookbook.

Use HTTPS and authenticate the client (e.g. session or API key). Validate amount and currency on the server; do not trust the client for the charged amount. Do not log raw token payloads; treat them like card data. Prefer creating a PaymentIntent (or equivalent) on the server and confirming with the token, so the server controls the amount and idempotency.

This cookbook shows how to use @gmisoftware/react-native-pay for wallet payments and process them with Przelewy24 on your backend. The library is not a gateway SDK. It only presents the native payment sheet and returns the payment token that your backend maps to Przelewy24 APIs. It follows the same contract used across this library: the app collects PaymentResult and PaymentToken the backend maps the token to Przelewy24 API calls

Przelewy24 REST docs (Apple Pay): developers.przelewy24.pl Przelewy24 REST docs (Google Pay): developers.przelewy24.pl Przelewy24 payment integration docs entry point: developers.przelewy24.pl Przelewy24 mobile library docs (registration and verification concepts): GitHub README Use Przelewy24's official docs as the source of truth for provider request fields, signatures, endpoints, and enablement requirements.

Complete iOS (Apple Pay) setup: Apple Merchant ID Apple Pay capability enabled on your App ID Payment Processing Certificate Confirm your Przelewy24 account is configured for Apple Pay. Test on a real iOS device with Wallet configured.

Complete Android (Google Pay) setup: enableGooglePay: true (Expo plugin) Google Pay API enabled in Google Cloud gateway config in app code (googlePayMerchantId, googlePayEnvironment, googlePayGateway, googlePayGatewayMerchantId) Confirm your Przelewy24 account is configured for Google Pay. Test on a real device (or emulator with Google Play Services) and a wallet card.
Implement a backend endpoint that: accepts token payloads from app clients maps platform-specific token payloads to Przelewy24 fields verifies and persists payment status

App displays wallet button (ApplePayButton on iOS, GooglePayButton on Android). User confirms payment in the native sheet. App receives PaymentResult (token, transactionId). App sends token + amount/currency/order data to backend over HTTPS. Backend calls Przelewy24 with platform-appropriate payload mapping. Backend verifies final status and returns checkout result to the app.

import React from 'react' import {ActivityIndicator, Platform, View} from 'react-native' import { ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton, usePaymentCheckout, } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import {callback} from 'react-native-nitro-modules' export function CheckoutWithPrzelewy24() { const {startPayment, canMakePayments, isProcessing} = usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', countryCode: 'PL', currencyCode: 'PLN', googlePayMerchantId: 'your_google_pay_merchant_id', googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST', // switch to PRODUCTION for live traffic googlePayGateway: 'przelewy24', googlePayGatewayMerchantId: 'your_przelewy24_gateway_merchant_id', }) const onPayPress = async () => { const result = await startPayment() if (!result?.success || !result.token) return await fetch('https://api.yourserver.com/payments/przelewy24/wallet', { method: 'POST', headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}, body: JSON.stringify({ platform: Platform.OS, // ios | android amount: 49.99, currency: 'PLN', orderId: 'order_123', transactionId: result.transactionId ?? result.token.transactionIdentifier, token: result.token, }), }) } if (!canMakePayments) return null if (isProcessing) return <ActivityIndicator /> return ( <View> {Platform.OS === 'ios' ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(onPayPress)} style={{width: '100%', height: 48}} /> ) : ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="buy" theme="dark" radius={4} onPress={callback(onPayPress)} style={{width: '100%', height: 48}} /> )} </View> ) }

Forward at least: token.paymentData (opaque payload; token format is platform/provider-dependent) token.transactionIdentifier and/or PaymentResult.transactionId order/cart identifier amount and currency optional platform marker (ios / android) to simplify provider mapping Do not parse or transform paymentData in the client beyond forwarding it.

Provider field mapping must remain server-side. Keep this as an internal adapter and follow Przelewy24 docs for exact request schemas. app.post('/payments/przelewy24/wallet', async (req, res) => { const {platform, token, amount, currency, orderId, transactionId} = req.body // 1) Validate amount/currency/order ownership server-side. // 2) Branch mapping by wallet platform. // 3) Build Przelewy24 request with required signatures/merchant fields. // 4) Persist payment status and return result. const p24Result = await przelewy24Client.createWalletPayment({ wallet: platform === 'ios' ? 'APPLE_PAY' : 'GOOGLE_PAY', amountMinor: Math.round(amount * 100), currency, orderId, idempotencyKey: transactionId ?? token?.transactionIdentifier, walletTokenPayload: token?.paymentData, rawToken: token, }) res.json({success: true, providerPaymentId: p24Result.id}) })

Always use HTTPS between app and backend. Never log raw token payloads. Validate amount/currency/order ownership server-side. Use idempotency keys based on transaction identifiers. Treat provider callbacks/webhooks and verification as the source of final payment state.

This package does not include a native Przelewy24 SDK adapter; integration is done through your backend. For production mapping and validation rules, rely on Przelewy24's official Apple Pay and Google Pay documentation.

React Native Pay is a unified payment module for React Native that supports Apple Pay (iOS) and Google Pay (Android) through a single, type-safe API for presenting native payment sheets and returning payment tokens.

One hook — usePaymentCheckout() handles availability, cart, and payment flow. Native buttons — ApplePayButton and GooglePayButton for platform-correct UI. Unified API — Shared request/result model across platforms; button component remains platform-specific. TypeScript — Full types and IntelliSense for requests, results, and tokens. Expo — Config plugin for Apple Pay entitlements and Google Pay metadata. Nitro Modules — High-performance native bindings.

React Native apps (Expo or bare) that need Apple Pay and/or Google Pay. Teams that want a single integration instead of maintaining two separate SDKs. Apps that already use (or plan to use) a payment gateway (e.g. Stripe, Braintree) and need the payment token from the device to charge on the server.

Check availability — canMakePayments from usePaymentCheckout() or HybridPaymentHandler.payServiceStatus(). Build the cart — addItem() / addItems() (or build a PaymentRequest yourself). Show the button — ApplePayButton on iOS, GooglePayButton on Android. Start payment — startPayment(); user completes the sheet; you receive a token. Send token to server — Your backend uses the token with your payment gateway to complete the charge. The library does not process payments itself; it gives you the token and metadata so your server can.

Renders native payment buttons (ApplePayButton / GooglePayButton). Starts Apple Pay / Google Pay sheets and returns PaymentResult + token payload. Provides hook-based cart helpers (usePaymentCheckout) and low-level API (HybridPaymentHandler).
It does not charge cards by itself. It does not replace your gateway SDK/backend payment flow. It does not bypass Apple Developer / Google Pay onboarding and account setup.

Platform setup (Merchant ID, entitlements/capabilities, Google Pay API/project setup). Gateway configuration (environment, gateway identifiers, tokenization mode). Server-side processing (validation, idempotency, charge/intent creation, error handling). Real-device testing on iOS and Android before going live.
Quick Start — Get a minimal checkout running in minutes. Payment flow — End-to-end flow in more detail. Installation & Setup — Prerequisites and platform setup.
This page focuses on runtime behavior and integration boundaries so you can make your checkout resilient.

The library does not charge the user directly. It opens the native wallet sheet, returns a tokenized payment payload, and lets your backend complete the charge with your gateway. At a minimum: App checks wallet availability (canMakePayments / payServiceStatus()). App builds a PaymentRequest from cart items. User confirms payment in the native sheet. App receives PaymentResult (success, token, optional transactionId). Backend validates order context and charges through your provider.

sequenceDiagram actor User participant App participant NativeSheet participant Backend participant Gateway App->>App: Build paymentRequest from cart App->>NativeSheet: startPayment(paymentRequest) User->>NativeSheet: Confirm or cancel NativeSheet-->>App: PaymentResult(success, token, transactionId) alt success with token App->>Backend: POST token + amount + currency + orderId Backend->>Backend: Validate order state and idempotency Backend->>Gateway: Create charge/intent using token Gateway-->>Backend: Authorized or failed Backend-->>App: Final checkout status else cancelled or failed App->>App: Show retry/cancel state end

With onAuthorize, your backend charges the token before startPayment resolves: on iOS while the Apple Pay sheet is still up, on Android after the Google Pay sheet has closed. The result below already reflects the charge, so don't send result.token to your backend again.
result.success === true result.token is present and should be forwarded to your backend. Your client should still wait for backend confirmation before marking the order paid.
result.success === false with result.error. Treat this as a completed wallet flow with a failed outcome (not a thrown exception). Show a recoverable UI (retry, choose another method).
startPayment() may return null when an exception occurs. The hook also sets error in state. Handle this as an app/runtime failure path (show generic error + retry).
Calling startPayment() with no cart items returns null and sets a "Cart is empty" error. Gate the pay button on items.length > 0.

PaymentToken.paymentData is an opaque gateway payload and is platform/gateway-dependent: Apple Pay (iOS): Base64-encoded data from the Apple Pay token payload. Google Pay (Android): Tokenization payload from Google Pay (tokenizationData.token), whose schema depends on your configured gateway. Always send the entire token object (or exactly the fields your gateway asks for) to your backend. Avoid parsing or transforming token payloads in the client.

Your backend should: Validate order ownership, amount, and currency from server-side order data. Use an idempotency key (for example transactionId + orderId) to prevent duplicate charges. Call gateway APIs with the provider-specific token mapping. Persist both wallet result and gateway result for audit/debug. Return a final, app-friendly checkout status.

iOS: Merchant ID and Payment Processing Certificate set up and installed in your gateway. Android: Google Pay API enabled; production gateway merchant ID and environment configured. Backend: Endpoint validates the token, amount, and context and uses the gateway SDK to create the charge. Security: Never log or expose raw token payloads; use HTTPS and secure storage for any sensitive data. Next: API: usePaymentCheckout or Server-side processing.
Get a minimal Apple Pay / Google Pay checkout running in your app.

Native button rendering and payment-sheet trigger. Getting back PaymentResult and token. Forwarding the token to your backend. This guide does not replace platform onboarding (Apple/Google) or gateway-specific backend implementation.
React Native 0.70+ react-native-nitro-modules 0.36.0+ (required) Android minSdkVersion 26+ (required) Expo 53–57 if you use Expo (SDK 57 requires Node.js 22.13+)
# Install Nitro Modules first bun add react-native-nitro-modules # or: npm install react-native-nitro-modules # Then the payment library bun add @gmisoftware/react-native-pay

Apply platform setup before testing checkout: Installation for dependency + setup flow. Expo plugin for Expo projects. iOS Apple Pay setup for Merchant ID and certificates. Android Google Pay setup for Google Pay API and gateway configuration. Bare React Native setup for manual native configuration. If you are using Expo, run npx expo prebuild --clean after plugin changes and rebuild.

Use the hook and the platform-specific button. On press, call startPayment() and send the token to your server. import React from 'react' import { usePaymentCheckout, ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton, formatAmount, } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import { Platform, View, Text, Button, ActivityIndicator } from 'react-native' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' function CheckoutScreen() { const { canMakePayments, isCheckingStatus, items, total, addItem, addItems, removeItem, startPayment, isProcessing, error, } = usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', currencyCode: 'USD', countryCode: 'US', }) const handlePay = async () => { const result = await startPayment() if (result?.success && result.token) { // Send result.token to your backend await fetch('https://api.yourserver.com/process-payment', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ token: result.token, transactionId: result.transactionId, }), }) } } if (isCheckingStatus) { return <View><ActivityIndicator /></View> } if (!canMakePayments) { return <View><Text>Apple Pay / Google Pay is not available</Text></View> } return ( <View style={{ padding: 20 }}> <Button title="Add Coffee ($4.99)" onPress={() => addItem('Coffee', 4.99)} /> {items.map((item, i) => ( <View key={i} style={{ flexDirection: 'row', padding: 10 }}> <Text>{item.label}: ${formatAmount(item.amount)}</Text> <Button title="Remove" onPress={() => removeItem(i)} /> </View> ))} <Text style={{ fontSize: 20, marginVertical: 10 }}>Total: ${total.toFixed(2)}</Text> {error && <Text style={{ color: 'red' }}>Error: {error.message}</Text>} {isProcessing ? ( <ActivityIndicator size="large" /> ) : ( Platform.OS === 'ios' ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(handlePay)} style={{ width: '100%', height: 48 }} /> ) : ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="buy" theme="dark" radius={4} onPress={callback(handlePay)} style={{ width: '100%', height: 48 }} /> ) )} </View> ) } If you are integrating with Przelewy24, follow the provider cookbook: Przelewy24.

ApplePayButton and GooglePayButton are Nitro views, so their onPress must be wrapped with callback() from react-native-nitro-modules, as in the screen above. A bare function does not reach the native button, and tapping it does nothing. See Troubleshooting: Nitro callback for onPress.

iOS: Real device with a card in Wallet; Simulator has limited support. Android: Real device or emulator with Google Play Services; add a card in Google Pay. For Google Pay, configure googlePayMerchantId, googlePayEnvironment, googlePayGateway, and googlePayGatewayMerchantId when you move to a real gateway (see Android setup and API: usePaymentCheckout).

react-native-nitro-modules and @gmisoftware/react-native-pay installed. Native config done (Expo plugin + prebuild, or bare iOS entitlements + Android manifest). Checkout screen uses usePaymentCheckout and the platform-specific button. Apple and/or Google account/platform configuration is complete. Backend endpoint validates order amount/currency and processes the token with your gateway. Idempotency and retry handling are implemented server-side. Real-device tests passed on iOS and Android. Next: Payment flow or Installation & Setup.
Configure your app and Google Pay for Android.

In app.json (or app.config.js), enable Google Pay: { "expo": { "plugins": [ ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "enableGooglePay": true }] ] } } Use the same plugin with merchantIdentifier if you also support iOS.

In Google Cloud Console, open your project. Enable the Google Pay API for the project. For production you will also need to register your app and comply with Google’s requirements (screenshots, business info, etc.).

Google Pay needs a Google Pay merchant ID for production, plus your payment gateway details (Stripe, Braintree, etc.) and gateway merchant ID. Configure them in usePaymentCheckout (or in your PaymentRequest): import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', // shown on the Google Pay sheet currencyCode: 'USD', countryCode: 'US', googlePayMerchantId: 'your_google_pay_merchant_id', googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST', // or 'PRODUCTION' googlePayGateway: 'stripe', // or braintree, square, adyen, etc. googlePayGatewayMerchantId: 'your_stripe_merchant_id', }) If you omit merchantName, the Google Pay sheet shows your app's label (android:label in the manifest). Supported gateways include: stripe, braintree, square, adyen, authorizenet, checkoutltd. See Google Pay Gateway Tokens for the full list and exact identifiers.
npx expo prebuild --clean npx expo run:android

Use a real device or an emulator with Google Play Services. Add a test card in Google Pay. For testing without a live gateway, use googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST' and a test merchant ID if your gateway provides one.

Button not showing: Ensure enableGooglePay: true is set, prebuild was run, and Google Play Services is available. Google Pay unavailable: Add a card in Google Pay on the device; for testing use googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST' and correct gateway config. See Troubleshooting for more. If you are integrating with Przelewy24, see Przelewy24 for an end-to-end app + backend flow.
Use this guide when your app is not using Expo config plugins and you need to configure Apple Pay / Google Pay manually in native projects.
documents.s: Bare React Native setup (no Expo plugin)

documents.t: In Xcode: Open your app target. Go to Signing & Capabilities. Add the Apple Pay capability. Select your Merchant ID (for example merchant.com.company.app).

Your app should contain: Entitlement key: com.apple.developer.in-app-payments with your merchant ID(s). Info.plist key: ReactNativePayApplePayMerchantIdentifiers with merchant ID(s). Example Info.plist entry: <key>ReactNativePayApplePayMerchantIdentifiers</key> <array> <string>merchant.com.company.app</string> </array>
In Apple Developer: Create/verify Merchant ID. Enable Apple Pay on your App ID. Create a Payment Processing Certificate and configure it in your gateway.

The @gmisoftware/react-native-pay Expo config plugin configures native projects so Apple Pay and Google Pay work without manual edits.
Add the plugin to app.json or app.config.js: { "expo": { "plugins": [ [ "@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "merchantIdentifier": "merchant.com.yourcompany.app", "enableGooglePay": true } ] ] } }

Option Type Description merchantIdentifier string or string[] Apple Pay Merchant ID(s). If omitted, Apple Pay entitlements are not added. enableGooglePay boolean If true, adds the Google Pay metadata to the Android manifest. Default: false.

iOS only (Apple Pay): ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "merchantIdentifier": "merchant.com.example.app" }] Android only (Google Pay): ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "enableGooglePay": true }] Both platforms: ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "merchantIdentifier": "merchant.com.example.app", "enableGooglePay": true }] Multiple Merchant IDs (iOS): ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "merchantIdentifier": ["merchant.com.example.app", "merchant.com.example.other"], "enableGooglePay": true }]
Run: npx expo prebuild --clean Then rebuild and run the app.

Configure your app and Apple Developer account for Apple Pay.

In app.json (or app.config.js), add the plugin with your Merchant ID: { "expo": { "plugins": [ ["@gmisoftware/react-native-pay", { "merchantIdentifier": "merchant.com.yourcompany.app" }] ] } } The runtime API reads this Merchant ID from the native app entitlements automatically. You only need applePayMerchantIdentifier in code if you want to override the configured value at runtime.
Open Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles. Create a new Merchant ID (e.g. merchant.com.yourcompany.app). Note it exactly; it must match the plugin and your code.
In Identifiers, select your App ID. Enable Apple Pay Payment Processing. Associate the Merchant ID you created.
documents.s: Enable Apple Pay on your App ID

documents.t: In the Merchant ID page, create a Payment Processing Certificate. Follow Apple’s steps (CSR, etc.) and download the certificate. Install it in your payment processor (e.g. Stripe, Braintree) as per their docs. The library does not process payments; your gateway uses this certificate to validate tokens. If you are integrating with Przelewy24, see Przelewy24 for an end-to-end app + backend flow.

Apple Pay shows the total as "Pay merchant". Pass your business name as merchantName: import { usePaymentCheckout } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' usePaymentCheckout({ merchantName: 'Your Store', currencyCode: 'USD', countryCode: 'US', }) The sheet lists your cart items and then the total line "Pay Your Store", which the library adds for you. If you omit merchantName, the total uses your app's display name (CFBundleDisplayName).

Use a real device with a card added in Wallet for full flow. Simulator has limited Apple Pay support; for production-like testing, use a device.

Button not showing / “Cannot make payments”: Ensure Merchant ID matches exactly, entitlements are present after prebuild, and the device has Wallet & Apple Pay set up with a valid card. See Troubleshooting for more.
Common issues and fixes for React Native Pay.

Ensure your cart is not empty. startPayment() returns null with a "Cart is empty" error when items.length === 0. Test on a real device whenever possible (simulator/emulator payment support is limited). Re-run native generation after plugin changes: npx expo prebuild --clean

On React Native 0.80+ (e.g. Expo SDK 57), the app can abort at startup with a stack ending in folly::dynamic::get<bool>() / BaseViewProps. Linking the library is enough; no pay button needs to be on screen. Cause: NitroPay.podspec defined FOLLY_NO_CONFIG, mismatching React Native core's folly config. Fixed after 0.0.16 — upgrade, then rebuild: npx expo prebuild --clean

Add a valid card in Settings -> Wallet & Apple Pay. Confirm the App ID has Apple Pay enabled and linked to your Merchant ID. For production, ensure your Payment Processing Certificate is created and installed in your gateway.

documents.t: Use only supported Apple button values: buttonType: 'buy' | 'setUp' | 'book' | 'donate' | 'continue' | 'reload' | 'addMoney' | 'topUp' | 'order' | 'rent' | 'support' | 'contribute' | 'tip' buttonStyle: 'white' | 'whiteOutline' | 'black'

Set enableGooglePay: true in your Expo plugin config. Ensure Google Play Services is available (real device or Play-enabled emulator). Render only the Android button on Android (Platform.OS === 'android').
Add at least one card in Google Pay on the device. Use googlePayEnvironment: 'TEST' for test flows. Verify googlePayMerchantId, googlePayGateway, and googlePayGatewayMerchantId.
Run npx expo prebuild --clean and rebuild. Ensure no other plugin overrides Google Pay metadata in AndroidManifest.xml.

ApplePayButton and GooglePayButton are Nitro views. Nitro passes a function prop to native code only when it is wrapped with callback() from react-native-nitro-modules, so onPress must always be wrapped. A bare function does not reach the native button: tapping it does nothing, and TypeScript reports Type '() => Promise<void>' is not assignable to type 'NitroViewWrappedCallback<...>'. import { Platform } from 'react-native' import { ApplePayButton, GooglePayButton } from '@gmisoftware/react-native-pay' import { callback } from 'react-native-nitro-modules' const handlePay = async () => { // Call startPayment() from usePaymentCheckout here } {Platform.OS === 'ios' ? ( <ApplePayButton buttonType="buy" buttonStyle="black" onPress={callback(handlePay)} /> ) : ( <GooglePayButton buttonType="buy" theme="dark" onPress={callback(handlePay)} /> )} Use this pattern anywhere you pass handlers to ApplePayButton or GooglePayButton.
Install react-native-nitro-modules (required): bun add react-native-nitro-modules. Rebuild after adding/upgrading the package.
